title: Reading γ
subtitle: what a gap between two clinics means for a patient
name: ModelInMotion_LogisticFE_E05_ReadingGamma
status: DRAFT: script under review together with its animatic.

segments.visual: The log-odds panel with Alder's and Cedar's lines. A bracket between them reads 0.87 and slides from one end to the other without changing.

sentences.text: Last time, every clinic got a line of its own, all with the same tilt.
Alder's line sits 0.87 above Cedar's. At the lower-risk end, at the higher-risk end, anywhere you look: the same 0.87.
sentences.say: Alder's line sits zero point eight seven above Cedar's. At the lower-risk end, at the higher-risk end, anywhere you look: the same zero point eight seven.

segments.visual: Beside the panel: a step of 0.87 becomes odds × 2.4. Then the question: 2.4 times what?

sentences.text: On the log-odds ruler, a step of 0.87 multiplies the odds by 2.4.
sentences.say: On the log-odds ruler, a step of zero point eight seven multiplies the odds by two point four.

sentences.text: So in some sense, Alder is 2.4 times Cedar. But 2.4 times what?
sentences.say: So in some sense, Alder is two point four times Cedar. But two point four times what?

segments.visual: Three cards, numbered 1 to 3, each finishing the sentence a different way.

sentences.text: Here are three ways to finish that sentence.
One: Alder has 2.4 times as many readmissions.
sentences.say: One: Alder has two point four times as many readmissions.

sentences.text: Two: at Alder, each patient is 2.4 times as likely to be readmitted.
sentences.say: Two: at Alder, each patient is two point four times as likely to be readmitted.

sentences.text: Three: at Alder, each patient's odds of readmission are 2.4 times as high.
sentences.say: Three: at Alder, each patient's odds of readmission are two point four times as high.

sentences.text: Only one of them is right. Pick one before we go on.

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: reading gamma.

segments.visual: Reading 1 as a header. Two rate bars: Alder 13 of 30, 43%; Cedar 8 of 20, 40%. A cross.

sentences.text: Start with the first, and count.
Alder had 13 readmissions among 30 patients. Cedar had 8 among 20. That is 43% against 40%: almost level.
sentences.say: Alder had thirteen readmissions among thirty patients. Cedar had eight among twenty. That is forty-three percent against forty: almost level.

sentences.text: And we already know why raw counts settle nothing: they depend on who each clinic treats.

segments.visual: Reading 2 as a header. Two rows of risk chips: lower-risk 18% and 34%, × 1.9; higher-risk 62% and 80%, × 1.3. A note: 2.4 × 62% is nearly 150%. A cross.

sentences.text: The second reading: each patient is 2.4 times as likely to come back.
sentences.say: The second reading: each patient is two point four times as likely to come back.

sentences.text: Take a lower-risk patient. The model gives 18% at Cedar and 34% at Alder. That is 1.9 times, not 2.4.
sentences.say: Take a lower-risk patient. The model gives eighteen percent at Cedar and thirty-four at Alder. That is one point nine times, not two point four.

sentences.text: For a higher-risk patient, 62% becomes 80%: only 1.3 times.
sentences.say: For a higher-risk patient, sixty-two percent becomes eighty: only one point three times.

sentences.text: And it could never be 2.4. That would be a chance of nearly 150%.
sentences.say: And it could never be two point four. That would be a chance of nearly a hundred and fifty percent.

segments.visual: Reading 3 as a header. The same two rows as odds: 0.22 and 0.52, × 2.4; 1.64 and 3.91, × 2.4. A tick, then the gap written as an odds ratio.

sentences.text: Now the third. Turn those probabilities into odds.
For the lower-risk patient: 0.22 at Cedar, 0.52 at Alder. 2.4 times.
sentences.say: For the lower-risk patient: zero point two two at Cedar, zero point five two at Alder. Two point four times.

sentences.text: For the higher-risk patient: 1.64 and 3.91. 2.4 times again.
sentences.say: For the higher-risk patient: one point six four and three point nine one. Two point four times again.

sentences.text: That is what a gap between two gammas means. For patients who look the same on paper, one at each clinic, the odds differ by a single multiplier: the odds ratio.

segments.visual: Cedar's and Alder's S-curves on the probability panel. A marker appears on each curve at the same risk score, joined by a yellow segment.

sentences.text: Here are the two clinics as S-curves: one shape, slid sideways by that gap.
Now slide a patient along, from low risk to high, and read both curves.

segments.visual: The patient stops five times. Each stop leaves a pair of dots on the curves and a row in a table: at Cedar, at Alder, difference.

sentences.text: A patient with a 5% chance at Cedar has 11% at Alder: 6 points more.
sentences.say: A patient with a five percent chance at Cedar has eleven percent at Alder: six points more.

sentences.text: At 18%, where Cedar's lower-risk patients sit, Alder gives 34%: 16 points.
sentences.say: At eighteen percent, where Cedar's lower-risk patients sit, Alder gives thirty-four: sixteen points.

sentences.text: At 50%, it is 70%: 20 points.
sentences.say: At fifty percent, it is seventy: twenty points.

sentences.text: At 62%, Cedar's higher-risk patients: 80%. That's 18 points.
sentences.say: At sixty-two percent, Cedar's higher-risk patients: eighty. That's eighteen points.

sentences.text: And at 90%, 96%: back down to 6.
sentences.say: And at ninety percent, ninety-six: back down to six.

segments.visual: The difference column is highlighted; a ratio column appears beside it, from × 2.2 down to × 1.06.

sentences.text: One gap, one odds ratio. But the difference in probability swells in the middle and fades at both ends.
The ratio of probabilities shrinks all the way: 2.2 at the low end, 1.06 at the top. Only when readmission is rare does it come close to 2.4.
sentences.say: The ratio of probabilities shrinks all the way: two point two at the low end, one point zero six at the top. Only when readmission is rare does it come close to two point four.

sentences.text: So what a gap costs in readmissions depends on which patients a clinic sees.

segments.visual: The log-odds panel with the four fitted lines. A yellow zero mark stands at the lower-risk position; a ring on each line marks where its gamma is read. Sliders show the four values.

sentences.text: Last time we said: read the gaps, not the gammas themselves. Here is why.
A gamma is read where every risk factor is zero. So far, zero has meant a lower-risk patient.

segments.visual: The zero mark slides to the higher-risk position, and the rings ride up their lines: every slider value rises by 2.02. Then it slides back to the midpoint: 1.01 above the start.

sentences.text: But that was our choice. Call the higher-risk patient zero instead.
Every gamma climbs by 2.02: the whole step.
sentences.say: Every gamma climbs by two point zero two: the whole step.

sentences.text: Or put zero halfway between, at a patient who doesn't exist. Now every gamma is 1.01 above where it started.
sentences.say: Or put zero halfway between, at a patient who doesn't exist. Now every gamma is one point zero one above where it started.

segments.visual: The lines have not moved. The bracket between Alder and Cedar, which travelled with the zero mark, still reads 0.87.

sentences.text: Through all of this, no line has moved, and no patient's probability has changed.
And the gap between Alder and Cedar is 0.87 every time.
sentences.say: And the gap between Alder and Cedar is zero point eight seven every time.

sentences.text: A gamma depends on where we put zero. A gap doesn't.

segments.visual: Two rows. All 103 patients at Cedar's level: 57 lower-risk at 18% and 46 higher-risk at 62% give 38%. At Alder's level: 34% and 80% give 55%.

sentences.text: One warning before we finish.
Suppose all 103 patients went to Cedar. The model says 38% would come back. All of them at Alder: 55%.
sentences.say: Suppose all one hundred and three patients went to Cedar. The model says thirty-eight percent would come back. All of them at Alder: fifty-five percent.

segments.visual: A log-odds ruler with the two average rates as dots, 0.69 apart. Beside it, two bars to compare: 0.87 for each patient, 0.69 between the two averages.

sentences.text: Put those two rates on the log-odds ruler. They are 0.69 apart, not 0.87.
sentences.say: Put those two rates on the log-odds ruler. They are zero point six nine apart, not zero point eight seven.

sentences.text: Nothing has gone wrong. The 0.87 compares one kind of patient at a time. The 0.69 compares two averages, taken over patients of very different risk.
sentences.say: Nothing has gone wrong. The zero point eight seven compares one kind of patient at a time. The zero point six nine compares two averages, taken over patients of very different risk.

sentences.text: Those are different questions, and the second gives the smaller answer whenever patients differ in risk.

segments.visual: One line of text under the bars.

sentences.text: So if a gap from a model looks bigger than the gap between two overall rates, that alone is no contradiction.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
A gap between gammas multiplies the odds, by the same amount for every patient.
What that does to a probability depends on where the patient starts.
And gammas depend on where zero is. Gaps do not.

segments.visual: A tag: 103 patients, rough estimates. Then the dial and sliders, drifting toward their fitted places; the next episode's title.

sentences.text: One reminder: every gap we read today rests on 103 patients, so each one is rough. How rough is still to come.
sentences.say: One reminder: every gap we read today rests on one hundred and three patients, so each one is rough. How rough is still to come.

sentences.text: And all this time, the lines have simply appeared, already in place.
Next time, we find out how the dial and the sliders settle where they do: fitting by balance.
